procedural_history.impugned_order: Common final judgment and order dated 02.05.2018 passed by the NCDRC in Review Application No.26 of 2017 in Review Petition No.3283 of 2008 and Review Application No.27 of 2017 in Review Petition No.2794 of 2008, which dismissed the review applications and affirmed its earlier order dated 31.05.2016.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The NCDRC initially passed an order on 31.05.2016 in Revision Petition Nos.3283 of 2008 and 2794 of 2008. This order was challenged before the Supreme Court in Special Leave Petition (Civil)…. CC Nos.24515-24516 of 2016. The Supreme Court, vide order dated 03.01.2017, refused to interfere with the NCDRC's view but granted liberty to the appellants-opposite party to seek review before the NCDRC. Subsequently, the NCDRC dismissed the review applications.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The legal representatives of the opposite party-sole proprietor appealed to the Supreme Court against the NCDRC's order dated 02.05.2018 dismissing their review applications. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals.

issue.issue_text: The jurisprudential status of a proprietary concern.

law.law_text: The Supreme Court relied on its previous decision in Raghu Lakshminarayanan vs. Fine Tubes, (2007) 5 SCC 103, which distinguishes a proprietary concern from a juristic person (like a company or partnership).

The Court also noted the definition from a 2020 Insolvency Law Committee report, which states that a proprietorship is not a separate legal entity but merely the name under which a proprietor carries on business, and the owner has unlimited liability.

application.application_text: The Court reasoned that a proprietary concern is not a company or a separate legal entity; it is simply the business name used by the individual proprietor.

Because the concern has no independent legal identity, the proprietor is solely responsible for its affairs. A suit by or against the proprietary concern is legally considered a suit by or against the proprietor themselves.
This principle extends to the death of the proprietor, where only their legal representatives can sue or be sued in respect of the business's dealings, as they represent the deceased's estate.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a proprietary concern has no independent jurisprudential status as a separate legal entity. It is legally indistinguishable from its proprietor, who is the real party in all its dealings and is solely responsible for its affairs.

arguments.issue_text: The jurisprudential status of a proprietary concern.
appellant_arguments: The legal representatives of a deceased sole proprietor are not liable to discharge obligations which were to be performed by the proprietor in his personal capacity, based on his personal skills and expertise.
respondent_arguments: The legal representatives of the deceased opposite party should be directed to comply not only with directions for monetary payments from the estate but also with the other obligations. Otherwise, the complainants would be left without a complete remedy.

cases.case_name: Ajmera Housing Corporation vs. Amrit M. Patel (Dead) through LRs
cases.principle: The legal principle for which this case was relied on is not specified in the provided text.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Upon the death of a party to an agreement, their legal representatives are accountable for the liabilities arising from that agreement, and the execution of its provisions must be carried out by the legal heirs.
obiter: An order of injunction is issued against a named person and is addressed to the defendant personally; on their demise, the cause of action ends unless the legal representatives are also causing a threat, in which case the cause of action continues against them.
A direction to pay money, whether by a final or interim order, is not considered to be an injunction.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The legal representatives of a deceased opposite party are not liable to discharge obligations which had to be discharged by the deceased in his personal capacity. An order of injunction is normally issued against a named person and is addressed to the defendant personally; on his demise, the cause of action comes to an end insofar as such a person is concerned. However, directions for monetary payments shall be made by the legal representatives from the estate of the deceased.
legal_tests_applied: Section 50 of the CPC, which states the extent of liability of a legal representative.

The principle that an order of injunction is issued against a named person personally, and the cause of action relating to it ends on that person's demise unless the legal representatives are also causing a threat.
policy_considerations: While complainants may be left without a complete remedy for non-monetary obligations, a party cannot be required to do or refrain from doing a particular thing that was a personal obligation of the deceased. The remedy against the legal representatives is limited to the extent of the estate of the deceased, primarily for monetary satisfaction.
